=== FILE: Behavior change and Motor Learning [cAJaH467zzY].txt ===

 col sixt sixt sixtus  change brought about by a cue or a new exercise or whatever it may be. We had Melissa Davis on the podcast a long time ago, and she made a statement that stuck with me for a long time, that real behavior change can take anywhere between two and six months. And the longer that behavior has been ingrained or performed, the harder it is and the longer it takes to actually overcome. So we accept that to an extent with things like nutrition, typical behavior change, that sort of thing. But people don't look at it through the same lens in regards to performance or movement change or the change in your squat technique. And I want to start really getting people to conceptualize that as a long-term process. A single cue is not going to fix your squat. A single cue is not going to put you in a better position in the bench press all of the time. So it's one of those things that we have to start to accept as a process and start really looking at habits, movement habits, communication habits, all those things as some form of behavior change. It's something that you have to do repeatedly over time to make stick. And that's really where motor learning comes in. You have to expose yourself to whether it's variations, whether it's well-executed technique or whatever it may be, and understand that you're going to have bad days that aren't necessarily going to look or feel the way that you may want them to. That's all part of the process. That failure is a learning opportunity for your brain. And you have to not just track those successes, but track those failures and understand that it's part of the process. So basically, in a long-winded way of saying this, what I'm trying to get across is if you want something to change, if you want your squat pattern to change, or you want to get better at deadlifting, or you want to, you need to understand that it's not going to take one weekend, it's not going to take one workout, it's going to take months and months and months of really, really dedicated training. That doesn't mean it's not fun. It's an absolute blast to do that stuff. But if you can conceptualize it in a healthier way, then we can start to decrease frustration when it comes to training and get more out of it. We're talking about breaking a habit, breaking a behavior, breaking an expectation or prediction that your brain is making, so that you can make an actual positive change, whatever that positive change may be, whatever your goal is, whatever's sailing it to you, right? So that, that's the key point today. Understand that these things take time. Motor learning takes time. Changing your squat techniques takes time. You may get a cue that clicks, and you go, oh, and you figure it out for a training session. And you go, oh, great. And then it's like a golf swing. Two weeks later, all of a sudden, it's gone again. That's because you have to continue to work on that and diligently work on that. And there's a bunch of ways that we can go about that whole process, but that's not really the point of this, this post or this video. So just keep that in mind. It's all about perspective. And that's the message for today.

=== FILE: Biomedical Model of Pain by Jared Maynard [SQwxKtMbNxg].en.txt ===

there exists multiple models which attempt to explain the what why when and how pain let's take a look at some of them first up is the biomedical model and this model assumes that symptoms are the result of tissue pathology and that there should be an organic explanation for all symptoms it would also assume a reasonably proportionate amount of pain relative to the tissue pathology and an example would be the Cartesian model of pain perception a picture of which is on the right-hand side of the screen now the biomedical model sometimes does a reasonable job explaining pain but it often Falls dreadfully short there are many instances of symptoms which have no apparent organic cause and we call these medically unexplained symptoms speaking of medically unexplained symptoms if you're feeling adventurous feel free to read the attached article symptoms in the body taking the inferential leap we also know that pain is often disproportionate to the amount of tissue damage sustained if there's any damage at all and if this pain model were accurate a phenomenon like phantom limb pain would not exist if the biomedical model is not wholly reliable in explaining pain then let's look at some other models which may be helpful

So what we have in this study in this meta analysis here is we've got a bunch of studies with vastly different samples. There should be some variability from rep to rep. You want the athlete to explore different positions to allow the most efficient movement pattern to emerge organically. And so as they kind of learn some movement patterns, let's say, you know, silly examples of catching the front squat with just a completely flexed turtle back really quick, you're going to learn that it's hard to support the barbell and you're, it's, you have more of a likelihood of dumping the bar forward. So you're going to want to catch it with your torso upright and your hips underneath you, but you kind of learn that organically. And then you, when you figure that out, the learner then discards the movement solutions that didn't equate to the outcome that they wanted. So the argument of these authors was, and then two, a lot of the coaching, the common coaching models are based around this coach centered approach, meaning the coach is in charge, the athlete just does. Coach says athlete does. And there's no, there's no back and forth involved. It's you learn it this way, you do it this way, because this is the way that I'm teaching you. And what these authors propose, number one, is to flip that into kind of an athlete centered model, where there's some feedback back and forth, the athlete has some say into what they feel and what works best for them. Within that, moving towards this constraints led approach to coaching, where instead of these memorizations, or memorizing some sequence of movement to learn, you set up the task to drive the movement solution that you want, without having to say a whole lot as a coach, you, you kind of set up the environment to allow the movement solution to emerge organically. And the athlete themselves just kind of works through that and figures it out. Now, I want to give some contextual background to a constraint, constraints led approach before we dig into the specific option, examples here in the paper. So constraints led coaching comes from primarily the dynamical systems model of motor learning. And within that though, there's ecological dynamics, which is this kind of psychology, sociology construct, how the organism interacts with the environment. So you've got this ecological dynamics model of the world. And then you've got this dynamical systems model of the world. And these two things have a lot in common. Dynamical systems came out of mathematics, statistics, economic theory, dynamical systems theory is a model to try to explain complex adaptive systems. And we've taken the dynamical systems model and ecological dynamics and tried to apply them to motor learning and motor skill acquisition. And there's been a big push for this. I mean, honestly, for decades, decades, but I would say, especially the last 20 years, we try to, this has become more mainstream to use the dynamical systems theory and the ecological dynamics approach to motor learning and a constraints led approach to coaching. So explains that a constraint is a boundary condition. And we have kind of three buckets of constraints. We've got constraints of the organism or the individual or the athlete, individual constraints. We have environmental constraints. We have environmental constraints. And we have task constraints. So individual constraints could just be modifiable, non-modifiable things of the individual, maybe output. Their range of motion could also be size, limb lengths, their weight, their cognitive and emotional capacity types of things. Environmental constraints can be the weather, the lighting, the temperature, the floor that you're performing the movement on. And then task constraints, rules of the game, the implement that you're using, the range of motion that you're moving through, all different types of things. So think of a constraint as a boundary condition. And the idea is that you can manipulate any one of those three buckets or all three in a myriad of combinations in order to drive the movement solution. So I'm going to stop there. And I want to make sure that everybody's still here. Kevin, can you hear me? Yeah. I still got you. Okay. Yeah. So anything to add from there? No, I think you summarized it well. I think the one thing that's important to kind of reiterate is that the constraints are not causing actions. It's kind of like, as you said, they just eliminate potential solutions. They kind of create boundaries or almost like if you think about like bumpers on like a bowling alley, it's not that the constraints are producing the movement. It's just that they're eliminating potential options. I think that's a helpful thing to kind of get across when it comes to perception and action and just how things self-emerge. Because that's the basic sort of baseline understanding of self-emergence is it's removing potential options to movement. But to add on that, I think it can work. === FILE: Knee Reconditioning For a Weightlifter with Knee Pain [NCfH1q9ojWQ].txt ===

 what's up guys, Quinn Heineck here, just a little clinical case, little clinical athlete, anecdote, for you guys, I'm currently working with a young weightlifter and his coach for reconditioning for some tendon-related knee pain that he's experiencing during snatches, clean jerks, back squats, etc. That's a great situation as far as a kind of a team effort, I've got a good relationship with the coach, we're in communication, the athlete's on board, it's just a really good situation, the only bad part is that he's experiencing that tendon-related knee pain which can be really frustrating for a young explosive athlete who just wants to enjoy training but also express his physical attributes and he can't do it, it's frustrating. So we're working on that reconditioning plan but one of the things that we're incorporating, especially in the beginning, I've been working with him and his coach for several weeks now, is a no-feet snatch, no-feet snatches are common place in weightlifting training, a lot of times for technique where we're looking to just kind of smooth out somebody's footwork if they've got kind of crazy legs or they donky kick or they jump back or jump forward, so a no-feet snatch is kind of a conceptual constraint that you put on the lift to try to smooth out the footwork and it can help smooth out the pull and it can do a lot of good things for technique but in this case, this athlete was sensitive to the landing or the kind of the reabsorption phase when the feet leave and then hit the platform aggressively, that was triggering the knee pain. So in this case, the no-feet snatches worked as kind of a buffer for that so he's still able to get the lift in but it's a little bit less dynamic, less impactful, less triggering of the tendon pain and in the beginning we're more closed with that prescription, a little bit more stringent with it as the symptoms were more reactive and I want to get to know the athlete and see how he's responding to the movements and so we're more strict on the no-feet aspect of it but as we go, what we actually want is for organic movement strategies to emerge that are beneficial for performance, yes, but also start nudging their way towards, you know, the competition style of lifting. Well, we had those constraints in place and he's, he's trained this way now over time and his body's kind of learned a new strategy so in this case he's able to work up to a PR snatch double across the board, no-feet-feet regardless and also in a, in a more comfortable position. Now, does that mean that over time, hopefully as we keep reconditioning the, the knees, we get stronger, more, more tolerance, more capacity that his technique won't gravitate back towards more foot movement and more of a deliberate impact in the ground? Yeah, it certainly might and, and fine, you know, we want whatever strategy is going to be best for performance long-term but in the short term it was just cool to see that that constraint that we put in place, we want it to kind of organically emerge into something else, you know, it starts to resemble that more competition form over time and that's what happened. === FILE: [ClinicalAthlete Case] Knee & Foot Pain While Squatting, Running, & Hiking [avvPsdy3D-g].txt ===

 What's up guys, quinn hennic, quinn hennic here of clinical athlete Newport, got another clinical athlete rehab case for you. This is a 33 year old male who works a desk job and trains for power lifting recreationally three times a week. He also attends periodic hiking trips once every one to two months. So his chief complaint is right knee pain with a previous diagnosis of tendinopathy. So there was no previous imaging as far as ultrasound to confirm tendinopathic changes, but he did have an x-ray which was totally clear and obviously that doesn't address the tendon, but he's got tendon pain which began in 2017 during a training period of high squatting and high hiking volume both combined. The pain is located right below the kneecap and kind of up under the kneecap, he says a little bit, and can also travel down below to where the insertion is at the tibial tuberosity. And it's aggravated with squatting, running and hiking. The pain increases with increased load and hiking mileage. And he reports that his hiking consists of zero mileage leading up to a trip and then a very concentrated dosage of mileage on the trip. And so currently the knee is not painful during power lifting training. So that's good, but he's keeping the loads below 60% of his previous one-rep maxes. So the weights are really light right now. And he does report fatigue with heavier loads, but it mentions that he shifts away from that knee or shifts to the left when the weights get heavier and or he feels fatigue starting to come on during the set. He notices that he unloads that leg. And then his secondary complaint is right foot pain also starting at the same time in 2017. The pain is located in the area of the sesamoid bone, kind of where the right MTP joint articulates there. And that's aggravated by hiking. It's not aggravated by power lifting training. And the pain is also dependent. It's a dose response. So it's dependent on the length of the hike and the degree of elevation. So the terrain has an effect on the foot pain. Objectively, we found right knee flexion, extension range of motion was all normal. His body weight squat barefoot had him do like 10 reps was no pain in the knee. I didn't really observe anything that would grossly say, wow, you know, movement wise, it looked like a pretty good squat. He hits below parallel. His back angle didn't really change all that much. He allows his knees to track forward naturally. Feet stayed flat. So there wasn't really anything to pick up there, which is not surprising because he's not feeling any symptoms and his pain doesn't really come on unless it's loaded anyway. We tested right knee isometric extension torque with a tensiometer at about 60 degrees of knee extension. It was an isometric test. And we found a 90% limb symmetry index. So his right knee is 10% weaker. And it also hurt. So when we tested that, it was a little bit weaker. 10% is not that bad, but it did create his familiar symptoms. And interestingly enough, I usually I have people do like a graded warmup set. So they they'll push 50% of max effort, 75% of max effort, 90% that will go max effort. And his 50% max effort actually also elicited symptoms. So at about 50 pounds of foot, about 54 foot pounds, he was feeling his symptoms already. So we've got some load intolerance there. Then we did a single leg decline squat. The decline was at 60 degrees and he was actually able to get 90 degrees of knee flexion to stand back up with no pain even on the right side. So that would actually surprise me. I didn't expect I thought that was going to hurt. He was able to do that though. As far as the foot, no, his great toe extension, ankle dorsiflexion, that was all within normal limits. There was no pain. I was doing, you know, passive overpressure was nothing. Couldn't really pick it up there. Not tendative palpation if I pressed right on the ventral MTP joint. We did a single leg calf raise barefoot for 20 reps to test kind of muscle capacity there. And he was able to get 20 reps on both sides. But he mentioned that the left side, he felt like he probably had five reps left in the tank. On the right side, he said maybe two. And he acknowledged that it fatigued faster. He also said that in rep number six, his familiar symptoms began to emerge. So right away, just in a single leg calf raise, he's able to recreate his symptoms that he also feels during longer hikes. So it makes sense. So, you know, the right tendon seems to be a little sensitive to tensile and compressive loading, as would be the case with tendinopathy. And we did note that mild extensor mechanism weakness, but the load intolerance less than 60% of one rep max was probably more significant there. Right foot pain, also an apparent compression and kind of dynamic impact intolerance. So both of these things, you know, stemming from spikes in training load, be it hiking or squatting back in 2017. And sometimes those things just stick around. You know, I wasn't, we weren't there to kind of see all the factors that played into it. It both confirmed that there's a capacity issue or deficit on that right side. You know, chicken or egg. We can't say that that's a causal issue of what he's feeling or vice versa, but it's a deficit that we found. And so, you know, some great exposure and some direct loading to those areas. It's certainly warranted. I don't plan on referring him out for any other imaging or referrals or ortho consult or anything like that. There's no need.
